My usual recommendation to those wanting to try out Linux is to use it in Virtualbox (https://www.virtualbox.org/) or another visualization program like VMWare. It's a program that lets you set up a 'virtual computer' running on top of your real computer's operating system. It's pretty easy to use and understand and there are tons of Youtube videos that can show you step by step on how to set it up. If you do want to try it, just download and install the proper version for your computer. Then go to a Linux distro site and download a .ISO file (virtual CD/DVD image) and save it to your computer. You'll need to get the proper version of the ISO (32bit or 64bit) depending on what your actual processor is. If you've got a 64bit CPU then you could run either one. In short, you'll create a new virtual machine, assign a portion of your computers memory and hard drive space to it, point it's virtual CD drive to the virtual CD that you downloaded and run it. It will act exactly like a real computer at this point and install Linux into it's virtual hard drive (it's really just a big file on your computer's real hard drive). There will be some things that you won't get the full advantage of such as proper 3D accelerated graphics, but you'll get sound, video, networking, everything basic that you'd get with your real computer. Using this, you won't have to worry about dual booting or possibly clobbering anything on your hard drive as everything you do in the virtual computer stays in the virtual computer. You can set up shared folders if you wish and VBox does have a one way drag and drop from your real computer (the host) to the virtual computer (the guest). If you've got enough hard drive space, you can set up as many virtual machines as you like and experiment with different versions of Linux. I'm currently using Linux Mint 17 but I've also used Xubuntu and Lubuntu (variants of Ubuntu but tailored to lower powered computers and using a more traditional desktop setting). This way, you can see if you like Linux or not and if you do, then you could install a copy onto your real computer. If you don't like it, then all you have to do is just trash the virtual machine. My current setup is Windows 8.1 with Linux Mint as a guest (typing this from Mint right now). I do my gaming in Windows and then when I want to do browsing, coding, typing, etc., I just fire up Mint.

  • Disable third-party cookies
  • Enable tracking protection (Firefox only)

  • Use HTTPS everywhere
